comments.text: The story file's header, 64 bytes, as the interpreter reads it: byte 0 the Z-machine version, 2 (save writes it and restore checks it); byte 1 flags, 0 (bit 0 set would stop the interpreter at $08C8); word 2 the release, 15; word 4 the start of high memory, $476C, whose high byte plus one, $48, is the count of resident pages (byte 5 is overwritten with $FF at start-up, $0895); word 6 the first instruction, $4859; word 8 the dictionary, $3686; word $0A the object table, $010A; word $0C the globals, $20DE; word $0E the start of static memory, $2CDC, whose page save and restore use; byte $11 bit 0 the SCRIPT flag the story sets and the interpreter tests; bytes $12-$17 the serial number `UG3AU5`; word $18 the abbreviation table, $00CA. The rest is zero. Story addresses are memory addresses less $2C00.

C-TABLE, the table of timed events, 180 bytes, thirty entries of three words, its address in global 116: INT finds the entry for a routine or adds one, working down from the end, and CLOCKER, run each turn, counts down the second word of each entry whose first word is set and calls the routine in its third word when the count was 1 or less; a count of 0 leaves the entry alone. All zero in the story as shipped: GO queues the first events.

180 zero bytes after the 180 that C-TABLE's routines use: the table's length in INT and CLOCKER, 180, counts bytes, and C-INTS can only go down from it, so nothing ever reaches these. They are the table's own second half: the released source declares C-TABLE as 180 words, which is 360 bytes.

The parse buffer that every sread fills, 240 bytes, its address in global 54: byte 0 is the most words the interpreter may write, $78 (120); byte 1 the count it found; then four bytes for each word, which leaves room for 59. The 60th word's length and position land on the text buffer's bytes 0 and 1, so its size becomes 1 and every later line is cut to its first letter: run live, sixty commas and then `open mailbox` give `I DON'T KNOW THE WORD 'O'.`. Only the one-letter words still work (`n` walks north, `q` quits); `restart`, `restore` and `save` arrive as `r` and `s`, so nothing short of booting the disk again puts it right. Past the 63rd entry the 6502's index wraps at 256 (the interpreter's $12EB): the next word's position goes into byte 1, the count, and its length into byte 0, the limit, so 63 commas leave a count of 64 and the story reads its last word from the commas in the text buffer, and prints a screen of memory as `I CAN'T USE THE WORD '...' HERE.` (live).

Finds the entry for a routine in C-TABLE, the table of timed events, and returns its address: entries are six bytes, a word that enables it, the turns left and the routine's packed address, from C-INTS to the table's end at 180 bytes. Runs the timed events once a turn: does nothing the turn after CLOCK-WAIT was set, which it clears; otherwise goes through C-TABLE from C-INTS, or from C-DEMONS in a turn the parser failed, and for each enabled entry with turns left counts one off and calls its routine when it runs out; an entry of -1 runs every turn. The story starts here: the header's first instruction, $04859, is this routine's first, after its count of locals, 0. Then it runs MAIN-LOOP, which never returns, and would start again if it did.

The turn, again and again: calls PARSER and, when it understood the command, carries it out through PERFORM, once for each object the player named (P-PRSO, or P-PRSI when the indirect objects are the many), printing each object's name and a colon before it when there are several, and stopping at one whose action returns 2. A walk is performed with the direction alone. A command whose pattern takes an object and was given none gets "There isn't anything to" and the verb. Then it counts the move in MOVES, clears P-CONT, the rest of the line, when the parser failed or an action returned 2, and runs CLOCKER.

Carries out one action, its arguments the action and the direct and indirect objects: makes `it` the last object named in this room, and says "I don't see what you are referring to." when `it` was named in another; remembers the action and objects for `again` (L-PRSA, L-PRSO, L-PRSI) unless the action is `again`; then offers the action to each of these in turn until one returns true: the actor's own routine, its container's (the room, or the boat) with 1, the action's pre-action from PREACTIONS, the indirect object's routine, the direct object's (not for a walk), and the action's own routine from ACTIONS. Then, unless the result was 2, the room's routine is called with 0, the end of the turn, and its result is the one returned. Restores PRSA, PRSO and PRSI as they were.

Reads one command and parses it. Clears P-ITBL and the object lists, then takes up the rest of the line that P-CONT kept, or prints ">" and reads a line into P-INBUF and P-LEXV; an empty line gets "Beg pardon?". Then it walks the words. A word not in the dictionary goes to UNKNOWN-WORD, and `then` or `.` ends the command, leaving the rest of the line in P-CONT. A direction alone, after a verb of walking, or before `then`, `.`, `and` or a comma is a walk, and an `and` or comma after it becomes `then`. The first verb goes into P-ITBL, its word into P-VTBL. A preposition, an object, an adjective, `all`, `one` or `a` starts a noun clause, which CLAUSE reads, two at most ("Too many noun clauses??"); a preposition at the end of the command is kept as the first preposition, a word other than those three followed by `of` is skipped (`bag of coins` names the coins), a buzz word is skipped, and any other word gets "I can't use the word '...' here.". A walk returns at once as action 105 with the direction in PRSO. Otherwise ORPHAN-MERGE completes the command the parser asked about, when P-OFLAG is set, and the parser returns true only when SYNTAX-CHECK, SNARF-OBJECTS, TAKE-CHECK and MANY-CHECK all do.

Asks whether a dictionary word is of a part of speech, its arguments the word, the part of speech's bit in the entry's flags byte (byte 4) and optionally the number of the part whose value is wanted: returns false when the bit is clear, true when no part is named, and otherwise the value, from byte 5 when the flags' low two bits name that part and from byte 6 when they do not: a verb's number, a preposition's, a direction's property.

Reads one noun clause for PARSER, its arguments the position in P-LEXV of the word that starts it and the preposition's number and word (0 when there is none). Puts the preposition and the clause's first and last words into P-ITBL, in the first or second clause's place as P-NCN says, and returns the position PARSER carries on from, -1 at the end of the line, or false when it could not read the clause. The clause takes in objects, adjectives, buzz words, `and`, commas, and `all` or `one` (skipping an `of` after them). It ends at `then`, `.` or a preposition, or after an object that is not followed by `and`, a comma, `but` or `except`, unless the object itself came right after `and` or a comma: such an object never ends the clause, which goes on to the next word; a word that is both an adjective and an object is read as an adjective when an object follows it. After `and` or a comma, a verb or a direction ends the command there: the `and` or comma becomes `then`. A word not in the dictionary goes to UNKNOWN-WORD, and any other word gets "I can't use the word '...' here."; either way the routine returns false, and PARSER stops.

It searches the room, when it is lit, and what the actor carries (DO-SL), first wherever the object could be and then, when that finds more than one, only where the pattern's search bits say. Then it decides. For `all` it takes all it found. For `a` or `one` it picks one at random and says "(How about the ...?)". When it still has more than one it asks "Which ... do you mean?", keeps the command with ORPHAN and sets P-OFLAG. When it found none it tries the room's global objects and pseudo-objects (GLOBAL-CHECK), and then says "I can't see any ... here.", or "It's too dark to see." in the dark. It clears P-NAM and P-ADJ when done, and returns true when it found what it wanted.
Zero, so that $05720 starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.

Searches the objects that belong to the room as a whole, for GET-OBJECT, its argument the table to add them to: the objects in the room's property 6 that THIS-IT? accepts; then, when P-NAM is a word in the room's property 5, pairs of word and routine, PSEUDO-OBJECT, which takes that routine as its action and the word's first six letters as its name; and when nothing was found, the objects in GLOBAL-OBJECTS.

Adds to a table the objects in an object that THIS-IT? accepts, its arguments the object, the table and how deep to go (1 everywhere, 0 the top level, 2 only inside what it holds): goes into each object that holds others and is open (attribute 13) or can be seen through (attribute 15), at the top level only when it has attribute 10, and through all of it when it has attribute 10.

Adds an object, its first argument, to a table of objects, its second, and counts it in the table's first word.

An object with attribute 12 is not taken, and when the bits also say it must be held (2), the object it could not take gets "You don't have the ..." and the command fails.

Refuses a list of objects where the pattern takes one: when there is more than one direct object and the pattern's first search bits lack 4, or more than one indirect object and the second lack it, says "You can't use multiple direct objects with '...'." (or "indirect") with the verb, and returns false.
Returns true when a value, its first argument, is in a table of words, its second: the words after the count in the table's first word, or with a third argument, words 0 to that number.

Returns true when a room, its argument, is lit: when it has attribute 3, when ALWAYS-LIT is set, or when something with attribute 3 can be seen in it, which it finds with GET-OBJECT's searches (DO-SL) with attribute 3 in P-GWIMBIT. In the room the actor is in, what the actor carries counts too.

Runs the villains every turn, one entry of VILLAINS at a time; the loop stops when its count reaches the table's, 3, so it runs the troll and the thief, and never reads the cyclops's entry. A villain out of the room is woken (AWAKEN), and stops fighting and being staggered (attributes 27 and 26), its action routine told with 1 when it was fighting. In the room, the thief busy with his loot is left alone for a turn (THIEF-ENGROSSED); an unconscious villain, its property 15 below 0, wakes (AWAKEN) when a roll of 1 to 100 comes under its chance in the entry's word 3, which otherwise grows by 25; a villain with attribute 27, or whose action routine says yes to 5, fights. When one fights, DO-FIGHT runs the round. Does nothing once the player is dead.
Wakes an unconscious villain, its argument: when its strength, property 15, is below 0, makes it positive again and tells its action routine with 4. Returns true.

Makes the sword glow, every turn the adventurer holds it: 2 when an actor that can be seen is in the room (INFESTED?), 1 when one is in a room an exit leads to (the room's properties from LOW-DIRECTION up of length 1, 4 or 5, whose first byte is the room), 0 otherwise. When the glow changes it says "Your sword has begun to glow very brightly.", "... glowing with a faint blue glow." or "... no longer glowing.", and keeps the glow in the sword's property 12. Once the sword is out of the adventurer's hands it switches its own timed event off.
Returns true when a room, its argument, holds an actor (attribute 20) that is not invisible (attribute 29).

Moves the thief, every turn. In the Treasure Room while the player is elsewhere, he puts his loot down there (DEPOSIT-BOOTY), first hiding again and showing the treasures (HACK-TREASURES) if he was in view. In the player's room, when the room has no light of its own (attribute 3), THIEF-VS-ADVENTURER deals with the player. Elsewhere he hides, and in a room the player has been in (attribute 28) he takes its treasures, three in four (ROB), and then ROB-MAZE or STEAL-JUNK. When he is out of sight, once a turn, he picks up his stiletto (RECOVER-STILETTO) and moves on to the next room among the ROOMS that is on land (attribute 2) and not sacred (attribute 19), hidden and not fighting, and tries again there. Last, outside the Treasure Room, DROP-JUNK.

Lets the thief drop what he finds worthless in a room, its argument: each thing in his bag but the stiletto whose property 12 is 0 is dropped, made visible, three times in ten (ZPROB 30), and in the player's room each one dropped says "The robber, rummaging through his bag, dropped a few items he found valueless.". Returns true.

In the player's room he says "You suddenly notice that the ... vanished.". Returns true.

Describes the room the player has just come into, as VERBOSE and the room's visits say, and what is in it unless SUPER-BRIEF is set.

Describes the room, its argument true for a full description. In the dark it says "It is pitch black. You are likely to be eaten by a grue." and returns false. Otherwise it prints the room's name, and "(You are in the ...)" in a vehicle (attribute 5); then, unless SUPER-BRIEF is set and no full description was asked for, describes it in full when asked, when VERBOSE is set, the first time (attribute 28 not yet set, which it sets) and in the maze (attribute 0) every time: the room's action routine with 3 describes it, or else its long description, property 11. Returns true.

Describes what is in the room, its argument true for full descriptions as VERBOSE gives: PRINT-CONT with the room, at level -1. In the dark it says "I can't see anything in the dark.".

Describes one object, its arguments the object, whether to describe in full and the level. At level 0, in a room, it prints the object's first description (property 14) until it has been touched (attribute 28), then its long description (property 11), or else "There is a ... here.", and " (outside the ...)" when the player is in a vehicle (attribute 5). At deeper levels it prints the indent from INDENTS and "A ...". Then it describes what is inside, when it can be seen (SEE-INSIDE?).

Describes what is in an object, its arguments the object, whether to describe in full and the level. For a room or a container it first prints the first descriptions of things not yet touched (property 14, unless attribute 25 hides them), and what can be seen inside those. Then for each other visible thing, not the actor or the vehicle the actor is in, it prints a heading with FIRSTER before the first, one level in, and describes it with DESCRIBE-OBJECT; a thing with attribute 25 is not described, but what is in it is. For the actor's own belongings every visible thing is listed. Last, what is in the player's vehicle. Returns true when it described anything after a heading.
Zero, so that $0612A starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.

Prints the heading above a list of contents, its arguments the object and the level: "Your collection of treasures consists of:" for the trophy case, "You are carrying:" for the actor, nothing for a room, and otherwise, after the level's indent from INDENTS, "Sitting on the ... is: " for a surface (attribute 10) or "The ... contains:".
Zero, so that $06192 starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.

Adds points, its argument, to SCORE and BASE-SCORE. When the score first reaches SCORE-MAX, 350, it sets WON-FLAG, shows the ancient map (clears its attribute 29), lets West of House be described again (clears its attribute 28) and says "An almost inaudible voice whispers in your ear, "Look to your treasures for the final secret."". Returns true.
Scores an object once, its argument: adds its points, property 13, with SCORE-UPD, and sets them to 0. Returns false for an object with none.

Its argument chooses "is" over "would be" when false, but every caller leaves it at its default, true, so the score is always one that would be. Returns the score.

Ends the game: tells the score and quits.

Reads a line after ">" and returns true when its first word is `yes` or `y`.

Kills the player, its argument the message that says how. Prints it, "Bad luck, huh?" when LUCKY is cleared, takes 10 points and prints "****  You have died  ****". The third death ends the game ("You clearly are a suicidal maniac..."). Otherwise the player is put down in the room, then, once the South Temple has been seen (attribute 28), wakes before the gates of Hell as a spirit (DEAD, TROLL-FLAG and ALWAYS-LIT set, DEAD-FUNCTION as the player's action) at the Entrance to Hades, and before that in the forest ("Now, let's take a look here..."). Scatters a dead player's belongings: the lamp goes back to the living room and the coffin to the Egyptian Room; each treasure goes to a room among the ROOMS that is on land (attribute 2) and dark (no attribute 3), going round them with an even chance at each, and anything else to a room picked at random from ABOVE-GROUND. The sword stops glowing.
Switches off the timed events a death ends: I-XB, I-XC, I-CYCLOPS, I-LANTERN, I-CANDLES, I-SWORD and I-FOREST-ROOM.

Moves the player on along a route, its argument a table of rooms in pairs: when LKP finds the room after this one, goes there with GOTO; false otherwise.
Returns the word after a value in a table, its arguments the value and the table, whose first word is the count; false when the value is not there or is the last.

Walks the player in a direction, PRSO, through the room's property of that number. A property of one byte is the room it leads to (GOTO). Two bytes are a message: the way is barred. Three hold a routine, which returns the room or false. Four are the room, the number of a variable that must be true for the way to be open, and the message when it is not. Five are the room, a door that must be open (attribute 13), and the message when it is not, or else "The ... is closed.". With no such property it says "You can't go that way.", except in the dark, where three times in four the player walks into a grue (JIGS-UP). A refusal returns 2, so the turn ends there.

Before `take`: "You already have it." when the actor holds it; "I can't reach that." when it is in a closed container (attribute 14 without 13); "It's not in that!" for `take` from something it is not in (and when it is, the indirect object is dropped from the command); "You are in it, loser!" for the actor's own vehicle.

Moves PRSO into the actor's hands, its argument false to do it without a word. A thing not already inside something the actor carries must not take the weight past LOAD-ALLOWED ("Your load is too heavy", and "... especially in light of your condition." when wounds have lowered it below LOAD-MAX). Carrying more than seven things, each more makes it likelier, eight in a hundred for each, that the second thing carried slips ("Oh, no. The ... slips from your arms while taking the ... and both tumble to the ground."), and is dropped. Otherwise the thing is taken, marked touched (attribute 28) and scored (SCORE-OBJ), and it returns true; a refusal returns false, and too heavy or a slip returns 2.

Before `put`: "Nice try." for a thing that belongs to every room (in GLOBAL-OBJECTS) or cannot be taken (no attribute 17).

`put` something in something: refuses what is not open (attribute 13), a container (14) or a vehicle (5) with "I can't do that.", and a closed one with "The ... isn't open.". Then "How can you do that?" for a thing put in itself, "The ... is already in the ...", and "There's no room." when its weight would take the container's load, its weight less its own size (property 9), past its capacity (property 10). A thing the actor does not hold is taken first (ITAKE), or refused with "You don't have the ..." when it has attribute 12. Then it is scored (SCORE-OBJ), put in and marked touched: "Done.".
Zero, so that $06B48 starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.
Would turn `drop` of the vehicle the actor is in into `disembark` (action 32), but nothing calls it: the pre-action table has none for dropping.
`give` something to someone: "You can't give a ... to a ...!" unless the receiver has attribute 18; otherwise IDROP, and "Given.".
Zero, so that $06B82 starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.
`give` someone something: performs `give` (action 47) with the two objects the other way round.

`throw`: IDROP, and "Thrown."; the thing lands in the room.
`throw` something overboard: in a vehicle (attribute 5) the thing goes to the vehicle's room, "... overboard!"; out of one, "You're not in anything!"; thrown at anything but `overboard`, "Huh?".
Zero, so that $06BE6 starts at an even address: a packed address can name no other.

Puts PRSO down in the actor's room: "You're not carrying the ..." unless the actor holds it or holds what it is in, and, when it is in something closed (no attribute 13), "The ... is closed." with the thing's own name. Returns true when it moved it.

Otherwise it opens it (attribute 13): "Opened." when it is empty or can be seen through (attribute 15); when it holds just one thing that has a first description (property 14), "The ... opens." and that description; else "Opening the ... reveals" and its contents (PRINT-CONTENTS).

Lists what is in an object, its argument, on one line: "a ...", with commas and an "and" before the last. Returns false when it is empty.

Counts the things directly in an object, its argument: ITAKE's test of how many the actor carries.
Returns the weight of an object, its argument: its size, property 9, and the weight of everything in it.
